summary:
NASA's SPHEREx mission maps the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared colours, imaging over a billion objects. Moving and changing objects, such as asteroids, brown dwarfs and variable stars, reveal themselves between images, but there is far too much data for any one team to search. Additionally, each exposure is taken at a different wavelength, so blinking images make steady stars appear to vary.

Ingress is a public web tool that lets anyone enter sky coordinates and watch that patch of sky change over time. Its default view compares the same wavelengths at every epoch, states exactly what was compared, and says so when no fair comparison exists. Users can explore all six infrared bands, zoom instantly, and click any object to measure its spectrum and brightness history with uncertainties.

On opening, Ingress demonstrates itself: from real SPHEREx data it recovers a 245-day pulsation period for the star R Draconis, matching the catalogued 245.6 days, while correctly reporting no period for steady control stars.

Ingress turns a vast archive into something volunteers, students and astronomers can search reliably, and share with a link.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Ingress is a public website for watching any patch of sky change over time in NASA SPHEREx infrared images. Enter coordinates and a date range, and Ingress finds every SPHEREx exposure of that field and plays them as an animation, so objects that move or change brightness stand out. No installation or account is needed: https://ingress-iuxy.onrender.com

HOW IT WORKS

1. Search: Ingress asks the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive which exposures cover the position.

2. Read: it downloads only the needed pixels from the public SPHEREx cloud archive, a few percent of each file.

3. Align: every exposure is placed on one north-up grid, flagged pixels are removed, and the sky background is subtracted.

4. Explore: the browser receives all exposures once. Switching wavelength, zoom, or frame grouping is then instant.

Users can choose any of SPHEREx's six infrared bands or a custom range, zoom to smaller fields, view difference images, and click any object to measure its spectrum and brightness history with uncertainties. Results can be shared as a link or downloaded as a spreadsheet file.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

There is a caveat. Each exposure records the sky at a different wavelength, so simply blinking images makes a perfectly steady star appear to vary because of its colour. Ingress separates the two questions:

- "Compare over time" builds each frame from the same wavelengths with the same weighting, so wavelength is ruled out as the cause of a difference.

- "Explore wavelengths" shows individual exposures, clearly labelled, with a warning that brightness can change with colour alone.

Ingress also says what it cannot do. It reports how many exposures and epochs support each comparison, measures how well epochs are aligned, and states plainly when no fair comparison exists.

HOW WE KNOW IT WORKS

On opening, Ingress demonstrates itself on real data. It measures the pulsating star R Draconis and recovers a period of 245 days (range 242 to 249), consistent with the catalogued 245.6 days. This is calculated live in the browser, not stored.

We tested for false alarms. An early version reported spurious periods for 4 of 14 steady stars in the same field. We added outlier rejection and a requirement that a period be found independently in two halves of the data; all 14 now correctly report no period. Fluxes of ordinary stars agree with the 2MASS and WISE catalogues to within 4 to 13 percent. A 12-page methodology paper in our repository documents every formula, threshold, and limitation.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

SPHEREx images over a billion objects, far more than professionals can inspect. Volunteers have already discovered most known brown dwarfs and many comets by comparing images by eye. Ingress brings that approach to SPHEREx for:

- volunteers and students, who can explore current NASA data in seconds;

- astronomers, who can check a position quickly and send colleagues a link to exactly what they saw.

New data releases are picked up automatically.

TOOLS

- Server: Python, FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy.

- Website: JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with no frameworks.

- Data: SPHEREx Level 2 spectral images from NASA/IPAC IRSA and its public cloud archive; 2MASS and WISE catalogues for validation.

- Hosting and code: Render, Docker, GitHub.

- AI: Claude (Anthropic) assisted with software development; an OpenAI model powers an optional plain-language reading of measurements.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: caveats sit beside results, and uncertain findings are labelled as candidates.

- Speed: five test targets are prepared in advance and open in seconds.

- Accessibility: built-in Help, About, and Methodology panels serve newcomers and experts alike.

- Reliability: test targets work even when NASA's archive search is unavailable.
